source_document.body:
Air cargo carries the world’s most time-critical goods, yet for decades it ran on paper, phone calls and spreadsheets. That is changing, and the industry now has the data foundation to do more with it.
The new foundation is AI. Not AI for its own sake, but AI pointed at the three outcomes that decide whether a cargo business wins: lower cost, higher revenue and less risk.
Building the digital foundation
Air cargo is a complex, multi-party business. Every shipment touches an airline, a forwarder, a ground handler, customs and often a last-mile carrier, each with its own systems. Connecting them all takes time, and the industry has been making steady progress.
IATA has made it a priority. At the 2026 World Cargo Symposium it noted that fragmented data systems still create inefficiencies, especially in high-volume segments like e-commerce.
That foundation is now well underway. The electronic air waybill has been an IATA standard since 2010 and sits near 80% adoption on enabled lanes. In January 2026, ONE Record became IATA’s preferred standard for end-to-end cargo data exchange, and airlines carrying more than 70% of global air waybill volume are on track to implement it.
With connected data in place, the next opportunity is putting it to work. Digitizing a waybill saves paper; deciding what to do with the data is what creates value.
The business case: cost, revenue and risk
Air cargo is a hard forecasting problem. Bookings come late, demand swings with the economy, and capacity on a passenger flight shifts with every bag and every gallon of fuel. Two weeks before departure, less than 40% of an airline’s capacity is typically booked, and more than half often fills in the final week. Spreadsheets and rules of thumb cannot keep up with that. Models can.
Cost savings. Across supply chains, McKinsey reports that AI-enabled management can cut logistics costs by up to 15% , lower inventory by 35% and lift service levels by 65%. In cargo terms, that means fewer manual touches, fewer re-keyed messages and less space flown empty.
Revenue optimization. In one McKinsey case , an AI tool cut a cargo airline’s demand-forecast error from about 20% to 14%. Predicting cancellations let another airline overbook with confidence, and together with other use cases it lifted load factors by around 8% after a 12-week pilot. McKinsey also estimates that raising below-average yields in the last week before departure by 30% can grow overall revenue by 7% to 8%.
Risk reduction. Yield volatility peaks in the final days before a flight, exactly when people have the least time to decide. Compliance is getting harder too: IATA counts more than 1,200 state and operator variations on dangerous goods handling.
Start with the business question, not the model
None of this happens by bolting AI onto an old process. McKinsey’s global survey found that only 37% of respondents attribute any EBIT impact to AI, and true high performers are roughly 6% of organizations. Adopting AI is easy; turning it into money is not.
That is why SmartKargo starts every AI capability with one test. Does it reduce risk, drive revenue or reduce cost for the airline? If it does not clearly deliver at least one, it does not ship.
Three principles keep it responsible:
People stay in control. AI recommends; qualified operators decide on pricing, capacity and exceptions, and can override any recommendation.
Recommendations are explainable. Each one shows the data behind it, the factors that weighed most and the model’s confidence.
Airline data stays protected. Encryption, role-based access and continuous monitoring, and data is never shared with other carriers.
Where AI earns its place in cargo
Air cargo generated $149 billion in revenue in 2024 , yet many critical decisions still rely on static rules, manual overrides and delayed reports. Four areas stand out where AI turns existing data into better decisions:
Revenue and capacity ( AIRCAM ). Forecast demand, predict sellable belly space and guide pricing, so more of every flight sells at the right yield.
Operations control ( AINOC ). Predict delays, flag shipments at risk of missing their SLA and rank exceptions, giving teams one clear view of what needs attention first.
ULDs and ground assets ( AIULD ). Track containers and equipment to raise utilization, reduce losses and know where every asset is.
Messaging and interoperability ( AICTX ). Translate and route messages across Cargo-IMP, Cargo-XML, ONE Record and customs systems, so data moves cleanly between partners.
Each use case works best when it plugs into the cargo systems an airline already runs, and when every decision stays with a person.
The bottom line
Air cargo spent years digitizing its paperwork. The next step is putting that data to work on the decisions that set margins: what to sell, at what price, on which flight. Airlines that treat AI as a disciplined business tool, measured against cost, revenue and risk, will pull ahead.
About SmartKargo
SmartKargo is the AI-powered, cloud-based platform that turns airlines into world-class cargo carriers, with cargo management, e-commerce, and AI in one system. Our cargo ERP runs the entire shipment lifecycle, from booking and acceptance to handling, tracking, and last-mile delivery. Our e-commerce solutions let airlines launch parcel products in weeks and connect directly to online retailers. Our AI applications forecast capacity and demand, guide pricing, and optimize load plans, so airlines capture revenue that legacy systems leave on the table. Trusted by airlines across North America, Latin America, India, and beyond, SmartKargo is making every flight a cargo opportunity. SmartKargo is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with key offices in India, the Philippines, Brazil, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and Canada.
See SmartKargo’s AI Portfolio to see how AI can turn your cargo data into better decisions.
